Objectives: The Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Winnemucca Field Office is proposing to decrease big sagebrush along roadsides in the Little Owyhee Allotment for fuels reduction and fire suppression purposes. The Little Owyhee Allotment contains some of the largest, most continuous sagebrush stands on the Winnemucca District. Fire has been aggressively suppressed within these allotments for over 30 years which has allowed the sagebrush to grow to large heights and the stands to become even-aged, with few naturally occurring mosaics remaining. This nearly continuous stand of vegetation would allow large wildfires to burn unchecked across nearly the entire area allowing it to destroy entire existing sagebrush stands, which in turn would destroy valuable wildlife habitat found in the area. By treating the sagebrush along the edges of the roads the BLM hopes to reduce the chance that a wildfire could spread uncontrolled and grow to large or even catastrophic size. Treating the edges of the road will break up fuel continuity and reduce overall fuel loading in specific areas creating breaks within the vegetation that will slow or stop an advancing wildfire.
Planned_Implementation: The herbicide (BLM Approved) tebuthiuron (Trade Name: Spike) will be used to reduce the amount of sagebrush along the roadsides by approximately 50 to 75 percent to create a wider and more efficient fuelbreak by reducing living sagebrush vegetation. Generally for the Wyoming big sagebrush plant communities, basal and crown cover is 20 to 40 percent. The crown cover for the Wyoming big sagebrush communities would be reduced 15 to 30 percent overall. Tebuthiuron specifically targets the brush species while minimally affecting grasses and forbs in the treated areas. The chemical (tebuthiuron) moves through the soil and into sagebrush roots; it moves up into the plant and will completely kill the plant within 2-3 years (Specimen Label for Spike 20P, 2003). Treated areas will be specific to areas where the sagebrush is in a late or mid-seral stage (see attached maps).\r\n5\r\nTreatment areas would stop one-hundred feet away from any existing open water sources (creek, cattle trough, lakes, and ponds) and from areas of exposed bedrock. Likewise, all other label specific requirements will be adhered to, including the avoidance of areas where groundwater is expected at five feet or less below ground surface (bgs). These untreated areas would be left as is; there would be no mechanical, hand, or other treatments in these areas.

Objectives: Weed treatments to prevent the spread of invasive and noxious weed species, including invasive\r\nannual grasses (medusahead rye and cheatgrass)
Planned_Implementation: The SW AT crew will make site visits, prioritizing sites with high potential for noxious weed establishment, and treat any small establishing populations with the appropriate approved herbicides. Application of all herbicides will follow given products directions for appropriate application rates (specific to species being targeted). All located populations of noxious\r\nweeds will be recorded (GPS'd and logged into a database) to track effectiveness (see below).
Actual_Implementation:
During the FY2015 field season, 65,453 acres of the Riley Field fire
were sprayed with an aerial application of Imazapic at 6oz/acre in
order to suppress the infestation of medusahead rye, which was,
and is, abundant within the fire perimeter as well as outside. A
buffer was used to treat areas outside the fire perimeter in order
to prevent reinfestation of the burned area after treatment.
Unfortunately, the initial treatment was only moderately
successful due to weather variables requiring a second treatment
during the FY16 field season. Between 2016 and 2017, an
additional 60,000 were treated with imazapic to attempt to
suppress the medusahead rye.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
This fire was originally on the former three-year plan format. Because policy at that time
prohibited weed treatments for ES treatment of invasive annual grasses, this plan was not fully
successful. Having to postpone weed treatments due to on-the-ground conditions of heavy
medusahead infestations negated most drill seeding opportunities and any success we may
have had in combating the infestation and establishing desirable vegetation. Due to this, we
opted to proceed under the established three-year plan rather than extend to five years under
the current plan structure.
We were able to utilize other funds outside of ESR to do our initial weed treatments necessary
the first fall after the fire (2015); however, those treatments were not as successful as hoped
and were reapplied in 2016 in the areas deemed most likely to recover naturally due to
remnant native and desirable perennial bunchgrasses and forbs.
The Environmental Assessment for the Riley Field ESR Plan was included with the combined
Buzzard Complex EA. This EA was completed jointly between the Burns and Vale Districts which
left both Districts vulnerable to appeal and litigation on a larger scale. Additionally, because of
differing resource priorities, the EA, with signed FONSI and DR, was more confusing than most
ESR EAs. I would recommend NOT doing joint ESR EAs or ESR Plans for this reason.
As stated above, in 2014 weed treatments for invasive annual grasses were not an Emergency
Stabilization priority and considered a pre-existing condition, which lead to less funding for the
treatments in, BAR. The Riley Field fire occurred in one of the most heavily infested
medusahead areas on the Burns District. The best time to treat this invasive annual grass, based
on research by the Burns USDA-ARS (research plots which were actually burned in the fire), is
immediately following fire, before the soil seed bank has a chance to germinate in the fall.
Unfortunately, we were unable to conduct these treatments in a timely fashion we determined
that we’d missed the windows for both aerial and drill seeding within most of designated
treatment areas.
Field season 2016 left us with no extra staff to conduct monitoring; however, in one year, and a
drought year, there were no significant changes in vegetation from 2015.

Objectives: Aerial Herbicide Application Fall 2016 (FYI 7) Boise BLM
Planned_Implementation: Additional areas will be evaluated for future imazapic treatments.
Actual_Implementation:
Based on adaptive management field assessments (See Part 6, S 13) and confirmed by
preliminary data obtained during USGS monitoring, the following modifications were made
regarding aerial Imazapic applications
3,800 acres of Succor Creek allotment pastures 2, 3 and 4, and Pasture 1 of the Jackson Creek
allotment were retreated because first herbicide application did not meet objectives and it was
determined a second treatment was needed prior to the drill seeding. (See maps Appendix D, S5
FY16).
• 8,060 acres of the areas drill seeded in fall of 2015 were treated in the Strodes Basin,
Sands Basin, Rockville, Blackstock Springs, Juniper Spring, Stateline, Jackson Creek,
Joint, and Reynolds Creek allotments.
• Approximately 8,900 acres drill seeded in 2015 were not treated with aerial herbicide in
2016; either drill seedings were progressing adequately without herbicide such that the
treatment was not deemed necessary (Rockville 1, portions of Blackstock Springs 1,
Juniper Spring 2, 3 and portions of 4, Stateline 1, Shares Basin 2, 6), or the annual grass
cover was deemed too high for aerial herbicide to be successful (Juniper Spring 1 and
Sands Basin 4).
• 10,580 acres of the areas aerially seeded with grasses in winter of2016 were treated in
the Blackstock Springs, Bush Ranch FFR, Jackson Creek, Juniper Spring, Reynolds
Creek, Rockville, Stanford FFR, Stateline, and Succor Creek allotments.
• 10,540 acres on steeper hillsides were treated to reduce annual invasive, release existing
perennials, and open up areas to seed sagebrush. Alkali-Wildcat, Strodes Basin, Sands
Basin, Shares Basin Juniper Spring, Blackstock Spring, Jackson Creek and Succor Creek
allotments.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2020 the foliar cover objective for the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment was met; mean foliar cover of annual invasive grasses for across all allotments and pastures was 16.2% (Table 8-51). Pastures with greater than 20% annual invasive grass foliar cover had less than 10% large-statured perennial grass foliar cover. In pastures with higher annual invasive grasses, Sandberg bluegrass cover was also below 10%. The one plot within the Wilson pasture of Reynolds Creek Allotment had the highest annual invasive grass foliar cover with 92. 8%, this pasture also had no deep-rooted perennial grasses or Sandberg bluegrass. Within all plots in 2020 in the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment area, perennial bunchgrass cover was 17.6%, Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover was 8.6%, perennial forb cover was 2.1%, and shrub cover was 2.0%.
In 2020 the foliar cover objective for the Fall 2016 Herbicide Treatment was met; mean foliar cover of annual invasive grasses for across all allotments and pastures was 17.2% (Table 8-52). Similar to the Spring 2016 Herbicide Treatment, pastures with higher annual invasive grass cover tended to have lower deep rooter perennial grass and Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover, though the effect was not as pronounced as for the spring treatment. Within all plots in 2020 in the Fall 2016 Herbicide Treatment area, perennial bunchgrass foliar cover was 21.0%, Sandberg bluegrass foliar cover was 12.2%, perennial forb cover was 3.6%, and shrub cover was 2.1%.
///
Monitoring Report 2019: 1. Foliar cover of invasive annual grasses is an average of less than or equal to 20%.
This treatment objective was met in 2019; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 12.54, varying from 3.04 to 16.25% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.93% varying from 0 to 32.66% in 2018 (Table 8-46).
In 2018 this treatment objective was met; mean foliar cover of annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in spring of 2016 across all allotments and pastures was 8.06, varying from 0.51 to 14.02% (Table 8-45). Pastures treated in the fall of 2016 had a mean foliar cover of annual grasses of 12.70% varying from 0 to 35.13% in 2018 (Table 8-46). Pastures that in 2017 had high invasive annual grass cover were not monitored in 2018 as the objectives were not met in these areas and were not likely to meet.
In 2017 the highest annual grass foliar cover was found in Pasture 3 (37%) of Elephant Butte, Pasture 2 (77%) and Pasture 3 (61%) of Hardtrigger, and Pasture 1 (65%) of Reynolds Creek. The herbicide treatment areas within these pastures were along proposed fuel breaks at elevations below 2,600 ft; areas dominated by annual grasses before the fire. These areas also experienced large amounts of annual grass germination prior to the herbicide treatment. This likely resulted in the low amount of annual grass control that was observed in 2016. The remaining areas treated with herbicide were above 3,200 ft elevation. Annual grass foliar cover in these pastures ranged from 0.51% in Pasture 4 of Hardtrigger, which is above 4,200 ft elevation, to 28% in Pasture 2 of Succor Creek, an area that is above 4,500 feet elevation but had high cheatgrass and medusahead cover before the Soda fire.
Based on adaptive management field assessments (Appendix B) that were confirmed by preliminary data obtained from this monitoring, portions of Pastures 2, 3 and 4 of the Succor Creek allotment, and Pasture 1 of the Jackson Creek allotment were retreated with herbicide to control annual grasses during the early fall of 2016 (8-46). These areas were chosen for re-treatment, because the spring herbicide treatment appeared to be ineffective, and they also had adequate densities of perennials on site to compete with annuals or they were scheduled for drill seeding to establish adequate densities of perennials. Areas dominated by invasive annual grasses, such as those mentioned along the proposed fuel break routes, were not considered for re-treatment with aerial herbicide.
When herbicide treatment areas were re-visited in 2017 it was observed that some of the areas that appeared to be failures were now showing clear signs of annual grass suppression. The most apparent example was along the fuel breaks within Pastures 2 and 3 of the Hardtrigger allotment. Treated areas had shown no signs of cheatgrass suppression in 2016, but suppression was very apparent in 2017. It is likely that the cheatgrass that had germinated prior to the herbicide application in spring 2016 was too developed to be suppressed by imazapic. However, the imazapic remained active in the soil and was clearly suppressing germination in 2017. It is possible that Jackson Creek Pasture 1 would have exhibit the “delayed control” however, it was re-treated with imazapic in fall 2016 to ensure a clean seedbed prior to drill seeding in fall 2017.
////
There were several important findings during inventory the first year post-fire:
Several new small infestations ( <0.1 acre) of leafy spurge were found within a 250 acre area near
Cow Creek. These sites were immediately treated and will continue to be monitored. No other
locations of leafy spurge are known to occur. No new invaders (new to the area noxious weed
species) were detected in the first year. Inventory provided a baseline of data for post-fire
potential spread of noxious weeds.
The majority of the rush skeletonweed chemical treatments occurred west of Highway 95 toward
the state line. Isolated plants were scattered south of Highway 78. Scotch thistle patches were
associated with ponds and springs. Perennial pepperweed was noted in Dry and Sage Creek
drainages. Whitetop was found east of Highway 95 from mile marker 3-7 and in the Reynolds
Creek area. Leafy spurge was noted east of Highway 95 near Succor Creek. Diffuse knapweed
was found at the old gravel pit near Highway 95 at mile marker 7 and Russian knapweed was
found at the bottom of the Poison Creek grade.
Re-inventory and monitoring completed throughout 2017 showed chemical treatments completed
in 2015 and 2016 were effective in most locations especially on small, new infestations.
Herbicide efficacy is a function of timing and environmental conditions. Many treatments were
very effective at controlling that year's growth however the large amount of moisture during the
fall, winter and spring led to ideal growing conditions for some species, especially plants that
germinated in the fall or the spring from an established "seed bank" like diffuse knapweed and
scotch thistle. This led to a significant increase in the number of plants especially in areas
where relatively few plants had been observed before. These ideal growing conditions were also
very favorable for deep rooted perennial species such as whitetop, perennial pepperweed and
Russian knapweed. Overall, chemical treatment has been very effective however many
infestations still persist and will need continued treatment to maintain control.

Following the all 2016 herbicide application the medusahead was controlled resulting in areas of bare ground.

S5/R5 Inventory and Chemical Treatment-Noxious and Invasive Weeds.
Noxious weeds are present in the burned area. Noxious weeds are now recognized worldwide as posing threats to
biological diversity, second only to direct habitat loss and fragmentation. Noxious weeds are known to alter
ecosystem functions such as nutrient cycles, hydrology, and wildfire frequency; out-compete and exclude native
plants and animals; and to hybridize with native species. The presence and abundance of noxious weeds in an
ecosystem is highly dynamic subject to changes in the local environment (Whitson, T.D., et al. 1992, Cal-Ipc,
2007). All natural communities are susceptible to invasion by noxious weeds.

Actual_Implementation: Aerial Herbicide Application completed in October 08, 2017\r\n(FY18).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
ESR Monitoring report FY22
Aerial Herbicide (Treatment S5)
In FY 2018 monitoring the aerial herbicide site, there was 0.4% invasive annual grasses, 9.1% deep-rooted perennial grasses and 16.7% Sandberg bluegrass (Table 7-2). The plots had a density of 1.73 plants per m2 and median basal diameter of 1.97 (Table7-1). Though the plots lacked the objective percentage of DRPGs, there is an established percentage of shallow-rooted bunchgrasses that provide forage for grazing. Further monitoring of these sites is required to determine the effectiveness of the treatment.
In FY 2019 monitoring the aerial herbicide site, there was 2.2% invasive annual grasses, 21.1% deep-rooted perennial grasses and 20.2% Sandberg bluegrass (Table 7-2). The plots had a density of 2.38 plants per m2 and median basal diameter of 1.57 (Table7-1). The plots meet the objective percentage of DRPGs for successful natural recovery but fail to meet objectives for density and median basal diameter.
In FY 2022 monitoring the aerial herbicide site, there was 7.1% invasive annual grass cover, 10.2% deep-rooted perennial grass cover, and 12.2% Sandberg bluegrass (Table 7-2). The plots had a density of 3.6 plants per m2 including seedlings and median basal diameter of approximately 0.5 - 2 inches (Table7-1). Since monitoring in 2019, DRPG cover fell to roughly half the 2019 value, no longer meeting the 20% cover objective. DRPG density has exceeded the original objective of three plants per square-meter, but basal diameter has not noticeably increased since 2019. Reduction of DRPG cover may have been due to the increase of invasive annual grasses. 2021 was a drier than normal year, impacting the establishing DRPG population.
Invasive annual grass cover has increased by 5% in 2022 and medusahead was detected for the first time in the Hawk fire boundary. Shallow-rooted bunchgrass cover has consistent since 2019. 2022 monitoring found that roughly half of this cover is made up of bulbous bluegrass (Poa bulbosa), a nonnative perennial grass with low forage value following early spring. Increases in bulbous bluegrass may be responsible for the loss of Sandberg bluegrass.

Objectives: Conduct weed treatments to limit the expansion of invasive species by treating\r\nmedusahead with a fall treatment of imazapic and conducting weed surveys to detect new weed\r\nsites and prevent old sites from expanding.
Planned_Implementation:
Currently, medusahead is known to occur in the area burned by the Riley Field Fire. Large amounts
of vegetation within the fire perimeter burned with moderate intensity, leaving areas of bare
ground, increasing the probability that noxious and invasive weeds, primarily medusahead, will
spread into previously unoccupied areas. These species will need to be aggressively treated to
eliminate the spread and prevent new infestations as the vegetation recovers. Although it is
unknown how suppression efforts or stabilization will affect the spread of invasive weeds, based
on observations following recent wildfires adjacent to the burn, invasive annual grasses establish
quickly and aggressively. Chemical treatment of noxious weeds will be completed under the ESR
Plan using separate NEPA that is in conformance with Vegetation Treatments Using Herbicides on
BLM Lands in Oregon EIS, ROD 2010. It is estimated that these noxious weed areas will require
three years (the first year under emergency stabilization activities) of treatment to detect and
control these species. There are areas (Map 6) where annual grass infestation will reduce seedling
establishment for both pre-existing native vegetation and seeding treatments due to invasive
annual weed competition. Sources that could spread weeds in the burned area are hunters or other
recreational users, wind, water, wildlife, and livestock.
Actual_Implementation: Additionally, the SWAT crew treated an additional 1000 acres of\r\nspot treatments within the fire perimeter.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The objective of the Camp Harney-Cow Creek Ecological Restoration Project is to remove western juniper and other conifers from vegetative communities where conifers are encroaching or have taken over desirable plant communities across the 16,201-acre Project Area. The conifer encroachment has led to losses of desirable vegetative communities, losses of wildlife habitat, degraded stream conditions, reduced productivity, and conditions that threaten the existence and perpetuation of bald eagle winter roost sites. Management action is needed to halt and reverse the impacts of juniper and to a lesser degree other conifer species encroachment.\r\nWith historic grazing practices (which removed fine herbaceous fuels) and the start of fire suppression activities at the turn of the century, the influence of fire in the Project Area was greatly reduced. Fire was the principal factor that controlled conifer encroachment into shrub-grassland communities in the Intermountain West prior to Euro-American immigration (110 to 130 years ago) (West 1999; Miller and Tausch 2001). As the frequency and size of fires across the landscape lessened, juniper expanded into shrub-grassland communities with an overall loss in ecosystem function and a dramatic alteration in historic biodiversity, hydrologic cycles, fauna, and nutrient cycling (Bates et al. 1998).

Objectives: For the purposes of Biotic Integrity Decrease Invasive Annual Grass To 10 Percent Cover of North African Grass, medusahead, and cheatgrass For 1-5 Years.\r\nA total of approximately 5,770 acres of BLM-administered lands would be sprayed with a pre-emergent herbicide (Imazapic-ALS inhibitor) to prevent establishment of Cheatgrass, North African Grass, and medusahead within the burn perimeter (Map 2). If the herbicide application occurs after germination of cheatgrass, a low rate of a foliar herbicide (glyphosate- EPSPS inhibitor) could be added to the application. Invasive plant treatments are necessary to maintain site productivity of native plant species and prevent increased fire recurrences brought about by re-establishment of flashy fuels such as annual grasses. The herbicide treatment would suppress annual invasives in the short term (1-3 years) and promote quick recovery of existing plant communities
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 5,770 acres of BLM lands are proposed to be sprayed with a re-emergent herbicide (imazapic-ALS inhibitor) in the fall/winter of 2021/2022 to prevent establishment of Ventenata dubia (North African Grass), Taeniatherum caput-medusae (medusahead), and Bromus tectorum (Cheatgrass) within the burned perimeter.
Actual_Implementation: Herbicide imazapic was aerially applied directly after the fire burned in the fall of 2021/2022 to 5770 acres.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: This treatment greatly reduced the B. tectorum and T. caput-medusae emergence this spring and allowed some natural regeneration of existing vegetation. Several infestations of invasive species were observed during ground surveys. These infestations consist of small populations of Bromus tectorum, Taeniatherum caput-medusae, Salvia aethiopis, Centaurea maculosa and Cirsium spp. Future ground spot herbicide treatments will be necessary to eradicate the infestations and it is recommended to continue this treatment. Weed populations monitoring and spraying of these sites should continue to reduce the spread of invasive species in a vulnerable burned area. New observed weed sites should be sprayed and monitored.
